# Greek and Roman gods — provenance report

<!-- Generated from authored/greek-and-roman-gods.json by scripts/authored_decks.py. Do not edit: change the dossier and rebuild. -->

**Deck:** [`decks/greek-and-roman-gods.ttl`](../decks/greek-and-roman-gods.ttl) · **Cards:** 43 · **Licence:** [CC0 1.0 Universal](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) · **Compiled by:** Anton Wiklund · **Created:** 2026-10-04

43 cards on 22 Greek gods: the twelve Olympians (counting both Hestia and Dionysus, as lists differ), Hades, Persephone, Eros, Cronus and five personified gods such as Helios and Nike. One kind of card asks for the god's Roman counterpart (Zeus → Jupiter), the other for what the god is god of (Zeus → the sky and thunder), in English and Swedish. Correspondences, names and domains from Wikidata and the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica, in our own words, checked against the Theoi Project and Swedish Wikipedia.

## Licensing

The deck is CC0 1.0. Its content comes from two sources whose licences allow anything: Wikidata, whose structured data is CC0, gave the correspondences, the English and Swedish names and most domains, and the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica, in the public domain (published 1910–1911, before 1931, in the US; elsewhere its articles used are anonymous or by contributors who died more than 70 years ago, see the source), gave the domains of Apollo and Persephone, the note on Dionysus and confirmation of the Roman names; facts and names are not copyrightable in any case, and the domain phrases are our own wording. The Theoi Project (all rights reserved) and Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) were used only to verify facts: every answer and note rests on Wikidata or the 1911 Britannica, no prose was copied from them (the Athena answer "wisdom, war and crafts" coincides with a Theoi title line, but is a plain list of three domains all given by Wikidata), and the selection of gods is our own (the Olympians and the gods named in the editor's brief, plus five personified gods with a one-to-one Roman counterpart), not taken from any list on those sites. The modern Encyclopædia Britannica was not consulted (britannica.com refused the request) and nothing was taken from it.

## Method

1. Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.
2. Finding the right Wikidata property. The brief suggested P2959, which is "permanent duplicated item" and does not link gods. The statements of Zeus (Q34201) were listed (query 1); the Greek–Roman correspondences are recorded with P460 "said to be the same as" (Zeus → Jupiter Q4649) and the god's domains with P2925 "domain of saint or deity".
3. Candidates. The twelve Olympians (Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes, and both Hestia and Dionysus, since lists of the twelve differ on these two), plus Hades, Persephone, Eros and Cronus, and the personified gods Helios, Selene, Eos, Nike and Tyche, whose Roman counterparts are one-to-one. Their P460 values with English and Swedish labels were fetched with query 2; Eros, Helios, Nike and Dionysus were looked up by their English Wikipedia sitelinks (API call 4), and the labels, aliases and Swedish sitelinks of all Greek and Roman items with API call 5.
4. Choosing the counterpart. P460 often lists several equivalents (Zeus: Jupiter, Thor, Amun, Indra and others). For each god the Roman deity among the P460 values was taken; where two Roman gods were listed (Hades: Pluto and Dis Pater; Dionysus: Bacchus and Liber; Persephone: Proserpina and Libera; Selene: Luna and Diana; Eros: Cupid via Q5011), the choice was made from the content sources and the other is mentioned in a note where it is common: Pluto, whose Wikidata description is "god in Roman religion, Plouton in Greek" and of whom the 1911 Britannica ("Pluto") says that among the Romans Hades "was usually called Dis pater ... and Orcus, although the name Pluto is often used" (so the card states this convention in its note); Bacchus, "ancient Roman deity of wine" in Wikidata, which the 1911 Britannica ("Liber and Libera") gives as another name of Liber; Proserpina, "the Latin form of Persephone" (1911 Britannica, "Proserpine"), Libera being only "sometimes identified" with her; Luna, "Roman goddess of the Moon" in Wikidata, Diana being Artemis's counterpart; Cupid, "Roman deity, counterpart of Eros" in Wikidata and "the Latin name for the god of love, Eros" in the 1911 Britannica ("Cupid"). The Theoi title lines agree with every choice but did not decide any (as first drafted, this step used them as the tie-break; changed in review round 3).
5. Names on the cards. English names are the Wikidata English labels (Cronus, Hephaestus, Mercury, Vulcan, Neptune, Saturn, Cupid). Swedish names are the Wikidata Swedish labels (Afrodite, Hefaistos, Persefone, Kronos, Apollon, Mercurius, Vulcanus, Neptunus, Saturnus, Amor), except where Wikidata had none: Dionysus (Q41680) has no Swedish label (only the misspelt alias "Dinosys"), so "Dionysos" was taken from the item's Swedish Wikipedia sitelink title recorded in Wikidata (API call 5, CC0) and confirmed in the article itself; Sol (Q1199937) has the Swedish label "Sol Indiges" and the alias "Sol", and "Sol" was used. Each Swedish name was confirmed against the Swedish Wikipedia article (API calls 9–11).
6. Domains. The domains of each god were taken from Wikidata (P2925 values with their English and Swedish labels, queries 3a and 3b, and the items' English descriptions) and written as a short phrase in our own words in English and Swedish, keeping only the god's main, uncontested domains. Apollo has no P2925 statement and is typed only as a "solar deity", a late identification; his domains (music, prophecy and healing) were taken from the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica article (fetched from Wikisource, API call 7). Persephone has no P2925 statement and Wikidata describes her only as goddess of the seasons and queen of the underworld; her answer (the underworld and spring vegetation) follows the 1911 Britannica article "Proserpine" (query 14). The Dionysus answer is "wine" (Wikidata P2925), with his vegetation aspect and ecstatic worship from the 1911 Britannica article in a note; the Tyche answer is "fortune", Wikidata's description (both shortened in review rounds 1 and 3, see there). Swedish answers name the domains in the definite form ("kriget", "kärleken och skönheten"), as Swedish names a god's domain with a definite genitive ("krigets gud"). No domain card was written for Cronus (see selection).
7. Cross-checking. Every card was compared with the god's Theoi Project page (fetched with query 6: the title line "… (Roman X)" and the first paragraph "X was the god of …"), with the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica articles (query 7 for the Olympians, query 14 for Pluto, Proserpine, Cupid, Liber and Libera and Fortuna) and with the first paragraph of the Swedish Wikipedia article (API calls 9–11). All sources agree on every correspondence and domain on the cards, except that the 1911 Britannica's article Dionysus names no Roman counterpart (its article "Liber and Libera" does) and that it says the Romans usually called Hades Dis pater or Orcus (see the note on hades-roman); differences in emphasis are recorded in the quality-control log.
8. The dossier's Wikidata checks (English and Swedish labels of every Greek and Roman god on the cards, the P460 link for every correspondence and P2925 values for the domains) are run by the builder against live Wikidata on every build.

## Selection

The deck covers the twelve Olympians (counting both Hestia and Dionysus, since ancient lists differ on which of the two belongs to the twelve), Hades, Persephone, Eros and Cronus, and five personified gods with a single standard Roman counterpart: Helios (Sol), Selene (Luna), Eos (Aurora), Nike (Victoria) and Tyche (Fortuna). Each god has a card asking for the Roman counterpart; each except Cronus has a card asking for the god's domains. Left out: gods with no single standard Roman counterpart (Gaia: Terra or Tellus; Hecate; Pan: Faunus is only partly equivalent; Uranus; Rhea: Ops or Cybele) and minor gods; the domain card for Cronus, because the common description of him as god of time comes from an ancient confusion of Kronos with Chronos, and he is better described as king of the Titans than as a god of something. Domains are limited to each god's main, generally agreed ones; later or contested identifications (Apollo as sun god, Artemis as moon goddess) are left out of the answers and mentioned in a note where helpful.

curl -s -G -H "User-Agent: solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)" -H "Accept: application/sparql-results+json" --data-urlencode 'query=SELECT ?p ?pLabel ?v ?vLabel WHERE { wd:Q34201 ?pd ?v . ?p wikibase:directClaim ?pd . FILTER(STRSTARTS(STR(?v), "http://www.wikidata.org/entity/Q")) SERVICE wikibase:label { bd:serviceParam wikibase:language "en". } }' https://query.wikidata.org/sparql
```

**2. The P460 "said to be the same as" values of the candidate Greek gods, with English and Swedish labels of both (sent to https://query.wikidata.org/sparql, Accept: text/csv).** (Wikidata)

```
SELECT ?g ?gEn ?gSv ?r ?rEn ?rSv WHERE {
  VALUES ?g { wd:Q34201 wd:Q38012 wd:Q41127 wd:Q40730 wd:Q37122 wd:Q37340 wd:Q39503 wd:Q40901 wd:Q35500 wd:Q44384 wd:Q41484 wd:Q41419 wd:Q41680 wd:Q41410 wd:Q45967 wd:Q44204 wd:Q131585 wd:Q178417 wd:Q213440 }
  OPTIONAL { ?g rdfs:label ?gEn FILTER(LANG(?gEn)="en") }
  OPTIONAL { ?g rdfs:label ?gSv FILTER(LANG(?gSv)="sv") }
  OPTIONAL { ?g wdt:P460 ?r .
    OPTIONAL { ?r rdfs:label ?rEn FILTER(LANG(?rEn)="en") }
    OPTIONAL { ?r rdfs:label ?rSv FILTER(LANG(?rSv)="sv") } }
}
ORDER BY ?gEn

**6. Fetch each god's Theoi Project page (Python script, User-Agent "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)", one second between requests) and extract the title line and first paragraph.** (Theoi Project: Greek Mythology)

```
URLs: https://www.theoi.com/ + Olympios/Zeus.html, Olympios/Hera.html, Olympios/Poseidon.html, Olympios/Demeter.html, Olympios/Athena.html, Olympios/Apollon.html, Olympios/Artemis.html, Olympios/Ares.html, Olympios/Aphrodite.html, Olympios/Hephaistos.html, Olympios/Hermes.html, Ouranios/Hestia.html, Olympios/Dionysos.html, Khthonios/Haides.html, Khthonios/Persephone.html, Ouranios/Eros.html, Titan/TitanKronos.html, Titan/Helios.html, Titan/Selene.html, Titan/Eos.html, Daimon/Nike.html, Daimon/Tykhe.html

Script run (python3 fetch_theoi.py). The title line is the page's text before the first paragraph; the first paragraph is the text around the first " was " in the tag-stripped page ("intro" in summary.json):

import re, time, urllib.request, html, json
from pathlib import Path

OUT = Path(__file__).parent / "theoi"
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
PAGES = {
    "zeus": "Olympios/Zeus.html", "hera": "Olympios/Hera.html", "poseidon": "Olympios/Poseidon.html",
    "demeter": "Olympios/Demeter.html", "athena": "Olympios/Athena.html", "apollo": "Olympios/Apollon.html",
    "artemis": "Olympios/Artemis.html", "ares": "Olympios/Ares.html", "aphrodite": "Olympios/Aphrodite.html",
    "hephaestus": "Olympios/Hephaistos.html", "hermes": "Olympios/Hermes.html", "hestia": "Ouranios/Hestia.html",
    "dionysus": "Olympios/Dionysos.html", "hades": "Khthonios/Haides.html", "persephone": "Khthonios/Persephone.html",
    "eros": "Ouranios/Eros.html", "cronus": "Titan/TitanKronos.html", "helios": "Titan/Helios.html",
    "selene": "Titan/Selene.html", "eos": "Titan/Eos.html", "nike": "Daimon/Nike.html", "tyche": "Daimon/Tykhe.html",
}
UA = "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)"
summary = {}
for key, path in PAGES.items():
    url = "https://www.theoi.com/" + path
    try:
        req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": UA})
        raw = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60).read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
    except Exception as e:
        summary[key] = {"url": url, "error": str(e)}
        continue
    (OUT / f"{key}.html").write_text(raw, encoding="utf-8")
    text = html.unescape(re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", raw))
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text)
    i = text.find(" was ")
    roman = [m.group(0) for m in re.finditer(r".{0,120}(?:Roman|Latin).{0,160}", text)][:4]
    summary[key] = {"url": url, "intro": text[max(0, i - 80): i + 600], "roman": roman}
    time.sleep(1)
(OUT / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=1, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")
```

**7. Fetch the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica articles from Wikisource (Python script, one request per title, one second apart). Hades, Persephone, Eros, Cronus, Helios, Selene, Eos, Nike and Tyche have no article under these titles; Hades, Persephone and Eros are covered under their Latin names Pluto, Proserpine and Cupid, which were first fetched in review (query 14).** (Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), as transcribed on Wikisource)

```
https://en.wikisource.org/w/api.php?action=parse&page=1911 Encyclopædia Britannica/{title}&prop=text&format=json&formatversion=2&redirects=1 for title in Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes, Hestia, Dionysus, Hades, Persephone, Eros, Cronus, Helios, Selene, Eos, Nike, Tyche

Script run (python3 fetch_eb1911.py); the article text is the tag-stripped parse output from the upper-case title onwards:

import html, json, re, time, urllib.parse, urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

OUT = Path(__file__).parent / "eb1911"
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
UA = "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)"
TITLES = ["Zeus", "Hera", "Poseidon", "Demeter", "Athena", "Apollo", "Artemis", "Ares", "Aphrodite",
          "Hephaestus", "Hermes", "Hestia", "Dionysus", "Hades", "Persephone", "Eros", "Cronus", "Helios",
          "Selene", "Eos", "Nike", "Tyche"]
summary = {}
for t in TITLES:
    page = f"1911 Encyclopædia Britannica/{t}"
    url = "https://en.wikisource.org/w/api.php?" + urllib.parse.urlencode(
        {"action": "parse", "page": page, "prop": "text", "format": "json", "formatversion": "2", "redirects": "1"})
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": UA})
    d = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60))
    (OUT / f"{t}.json").write_text(json.dumps(d, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")
    if "error" in d:
        summary[t] = {"page": page, "error": d["error"]["info"]}
        continue
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", html.unescape(re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", d["parse"]["text"])))
    i = text.find(t.upper())
    summary[t] = {"page": d["parse"]["title"], "start": text[max(0, i): i + 900],
                  "roman": [m.group(0) for m in re.finditer(r".{0,150}(?:Roman|Latin|identified).{0,150}", text)][:5]}
    time.sleep(1)
(OUT / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=1, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")
```

**14. Review rounds 1–3: further 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica articles (the gods outside the Olympians are filed under their Latin names), and a re-fetch of the Olympian articles to read their contributors' signatures. Script eb.py, run as: python3 eb.py Proserpine Pluto Fortuna Fortune; python3 eb.py Zeus Hera Poseidon Demeter Athena Apollo Artemis Ares Aphrodite Hephaestus Hermes Hestia Dionysus; python3 eb.py Cupid Liber Luna Bacchus Orcus (Fortune and Orcus do not exist; Bacchus redirects to Dionysus; Luna has no relevant text).** (Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), as transcribed on Wikisource)

```
import json, re, sys, time, urllib.parse, urllib.request, html

UA = "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)"
OUT = "/tmp/claude-1000/-home-antwika-dev-github-antwika-solid-memo/29afcb49-8c27-4a6e-be7b-e04afdd93785/scratchpad/greek-and-roman-gods/qc1/"

for title in sys.argv[1:]:
    url = ("https://en.wikisource.org/w/api.php?action=parse&page="
           + urllib.parse.quote("1911 Encyclopædia Britannica/" + title)
           + "&prop=text&format=json&formatversion=2&redirects=1")
    print("URL:", url)
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": UA})
    data = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req))
    if "error" in data:
        print(title, "ERROR", data["error"].get("info"))
        continue
    raw = data["parse"]["text"]
    text = html.unescape(re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", raw))
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text)
    open(OUT + "eb-" + title.replace(" ", "_") + ".txt", "w").write(text)
    print("==", title, len(text))
    print(text[:6000])
    time.sleep(1)
```

## Quality control

5 rounds, 34 findings: 29 fixed, 1 rejected after checking, 4 needing no change. Every card's Wikidata checks (138 in all) are re-run against live Wikidata by `scripts/authored_decks.py check` before every build.

### Round 0: Machine checks against Wikidata and cross-checks of every card against the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica, the Theoi Project and Swedish Wikipedia (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — authoring agent, machine checks · **Scope:** All 43 cards, the property used for the correspondences, the Swedish names and the deck's licensing.

The builder's Wikidata checks cover the English and Swedish labels or aliases of every Greek and Roman god named on the cards (except the Swedish name Dionysos, which Wikidata lacks), the P460 link from each Greek god to the Roman counterpart on the card, and P2925 values for the domains where Wikidata has them. Every correspondence agrees across Wikidata, Theoi and Swedish Wikipedia (and the 1911 Britannica for the Olympians). The discrepancies found and how they were resolved are listed below.

Three warnings (the Pluto convention, and "spring growth" and "festivity" resting only on verification sources) and two suggestions (the god count in the description, a Hestia check).
